decks.title: Business Finance — Part 1: Need for Finance, Sources and Financial Planning
goals: Explain why a business needs finance at every stage
Compare the sources of finance open to a sole trader, a partnership and a company
Explain the meaning, features and importance of financial planning

slides.heading: Business Finance, Financial Planning and Capital
slides.body_md: Part 1: why business needs **finance**, the **sources** open to each form of business, and **financial planning**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: why business needs finance, sources for each form of business, and financial planning
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Every business, from a roadside bakery to a giant solar company, runs on money. In this part we see why finance is needed, where each type of business can find it, and how a financial plan makes sure the money is there at the right time.

slides.heading: Why business needs finance
slides.body_md: Finance is the **lifeblood** of business: it is needed to **start**, to **run**, to **grow** and to **meet shocks**.

visual.alt: Flow showing four stages at which a business needs finance: to start, to run day to day, to grow or modernise, and to meet sudden shocks
visual.caption: Finance is needed at every stage, not only at the start.

slides.narration: A business needs money before it earns any, to buy land, machines and licences. It needs money every day to buy materials and pay wages and bills. It needs fresh money to expand or modernise. And it needs a reserve to survive sudden shocks such as a flood or a lost customer.

slides.heading: Quick check: only at the start?
slides.body_md: True or false: a business needs finance only when it is started.
slides.narration: Think of the four stages on the last slide.

slides.heading: Sources by form of business

rows: Loans from relatives or a bank on personal credit; trade credit
Partners' capital; admitting a new partner
Partners' loans; bank loans; trade credit
Equity and preference shares; retained earnings
Debentures; public deposits; loans from banks and institutions; trade credit

visual.alt: Table comparing owners' funds and borrowed funds available to a sole proprietorship, a partnership and a joint stock company

slides.narration: Who owns the business decides where it can find money. A sole trader relies on personal savings and personal credit. A partnership can add partners' capital, admit new partners and borrow. A company can sell shares and debentures to the public, retain profits and take large loans. Trade credit is open to all.

A wider ownership base means larger funds
visual.caption: The wider the ownership base, the larger the funds a business can raise.

slides.narration: Picture three bars. A sole trader has the narrowest base: one person's savings and credit. A partnership is wider, with several partners. A company is widest, because it can sell shares and debentures to thousands of investors. That is why big projects are usually run by companies.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: matching need and source
bullets: Step 1: identify the **form** of business.
Step 2: judge the **size** and **period** of the need.
Step 3: pick a source open to that form and explain why.

rows: Owner's savings plus a small bank loan
New lens plant for Lonar Lenses Ltd

visual.alt: Worked table matching three imagined needs to a form of business, a sensible source and the reason
visual.caption: Ask: who owns the firm, how much is needed, and for how long?

slides.narration: A bakery owner wanting a second oven can use her savings and a small bank loan, keeping full control. A travel partnership wanting buses can admit a new partner, bringing capital with no interest. A lens company building a plant needs a very large, long-term sum, so it can issue shares and debentures.

slides.heading: Quick check: a sole trader's options
slides.body_md: Which source is **not** open to a sole trader?
slides.narration: Which source belongs only to companies?

slides.heading: What is financial planning?
slides.body_md: **Financial planning** prepares a **blueprint** of future money needs: **how much**, **when**, and **from where**. Its twin aims: funds **when needed**, and **no idle surplus**.

visual.alt: Flow of financial planning: estimate needs, time them, choose sources, and review and revise
visual.caption: A plan is reviewed as conditions change.

slides.narration: Financial planning looks ahead. It estimates how much money the business will need, when it will need it, and where it will come from. It has two aims. Money must be ready when it is needed, and the firm must not raise more than it needs, because idle money still costs interest.

slides.heading: Features of a sound financial plan

rows: Can managers understand and follow it?
Does it look ahead to future needs?
Can it be adjusted when costs or sales change?
Is every rupee put to productive use?
Is there enough cash for current payments?
Are funds raised at the lowest suitable cost?

visual.alt: Table of six features of a sound financial plan with the question each feature asks

slides.narration: A good plan is simple, so that managers can follow it. It shows foresight, looking well ahead. It is flexible, so that it can change with costs and sales. It puts funds to their best use, keeps enough cash for current bills, and raises money at the lowest suitable cost.

slides.heading: Quick check: a standby limit
slides.body_md: A houseboat firm's plan includes a standby bank limit for sudden repair costs. Which feature is this?
slides.narration: Can the plan bend when costs change?

slides.heading: Why financial planning matters

rows: A cashew unit arranges a loan before the harvest
A software firm borrows only what its project costs
A new machine is matched with a suitable loan
A houseboat firm keeps a standby limit
Actual spending is compared with monthly targets

visual.alt: Table of six benefits of financial planning, each with an imagined illustration

slides.narration: Financial planning brings six benefits. Funds arrive when needed. No unnecessary money is raised. Investment and financing decisions are linked. The firm is ready for surprises. Managers can compare actual spending with the plan. And waste and duplication between departments fall.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a seasonal cash plan
slides.body_md: An imagined sweater maker in Ooty sells mostly from October to January.
bullets: Step 1: list expected **cash in** and **cash out** each month.
Step 2: find the **gap** (October: 17 − 9 = ₹8 lakh short).
Step 3: plan a **source** for the gap and a **repayment** date.

rows: Draw ₹8 lakh from a seasonal loan
Clear the loan; review next year

visual.alt: Worked month-by-month cash plan of an imagined sweater maker: in October cash out exceeds cash in by eight lakh rupees, met by a seasonal loan that is repaid in November and December
visual.caption: Imagined cash plan of Nilgiri Knitwear, Ooty.

slides.narration: Here the firm spends heavily in October on wool and wages, before festival sales come in. The plan shows an eight lakh rupee gap, so it arranges a seasonal loan in advance. As sales pour in during November and December, it repays the loan instead of letting surplus cash lie idle.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Needed to start, run, grow and meet shocks
Shares, debentures, retained earnings, deposits, loans
Blueprint: how much, when, from where

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: finance, sources for each form of business and financial planning

slides.narration: To sum up. Finance is needed to start, run, grow and survive shocks. A sole trader relies on personal savings and credit, a partnership on its partners, and a company can tap the public. Financial planning is a blueprint of how much money is needed, when and from where.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Always check the **form of business** before naming a source.
Learn the two **objectives** of financial planning: funds when needed; no idle surplus.
For features, use the case words: **simple, look ahead, flexible, liquid, economical**.
Link each point to the **firm in the question**.

visual.alt: Three steps for case questions: quote the fact, name the factor, and state its effect

slides.narration: Some tips. Before naming a source, check whether the firm is a sole trader, a partnership or a company. Remember the two objectives of financial planning. When a case describes a plan, look for the clue words that reveal each feature, and always tie your answer to the firm.

decks.title: Business Finance — Part 2: Capital Structure, Fixed Capital and Working Capital
goals: Discuss the factors that decide the mix of debt and equity, including trading on equity
Explain the factors affecting fixed capital requirements
Distinguish types of working capital, explain its factors and compare it with fixed capital

slides.heading: Capital Structure, Fixed and Working Capital
slides.body_md: Part 2: the **mix** of debt and equity, **trading on equity**, and how much **fixed** and **working** capital a firm needs.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: capital structure, trading on equity, fixed capital and working capital
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In this part we ask two questions. How should a company mix borrowed money and owners' money? And how much does it need for long-term assets and for day-to-day running? The answers depend on factors you can spot in any case.

slides.heading: Capital structure: debt or equity?
slides.body_md: **Capital structure** is the proportion of **debt** (borrowed funds) and **equity** (owners' funds) in long-term finance.

slides.narration: Think of a balance. Debt is cheaper, because interest saves tax, and lenders get no vote. But interest is a fixed charge, so more debt means more risk. Equity has no fixed charge, but it costs more and brings in new voting owners. The right mix balances these.

slides.heading: Factors affecting capital structure

rows: Interest is low and the tax rate is high
Return exceeds the interest rate (trading on equity)
Cash inflows are steady and strong
Owners do not want new voting shareholders

visual.alt: Table of seven factors affecting capital structure and the condition under which each favours more debt

slides.narration: Seven factors guide the choice. The cost of debt and the tax rate. Whether the return on investment beats the interest rate. How steady the cash flow is. The level of business risk. Whether owners want to keep control. The need to keep some borrowing power in reserve. And the state of the share market.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: trading on equity
slides.body_md: An imagined glass company needs ₹40,00,000. EBIT ₹8,00,000; tax 25 per cent.
bullets: Step 1: deduct **interest** to get profit before tax.
Step 2: deduct **tax** to get profit after tax.
Step 3: divide by the **number of equity shares**.

visual.alt: Worked table for an imagined glass company raising forty lakh rupees: with EBIT of eight lakh, Plan A (all equity) gives EPS of one rupee fifty, Plan B (half debt at ten per cent) gives EPS of two rupees twenty-five
visual.caption: Imagined: Godavari Glassworks Ltd. Return on capital 20 per cent > interest 10 per cent, so debt lifts EPS.

slides.narration: Plan A uses only equity. Plan B borrows half at ten per cent. Under Plan B the interest is two lakh rupees, but there are only half as many shares. Because the company earns twenty per cent on its capital, double the interest rate, earnings per share rise from one rupee fifty to two rupees twenty five.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: when debt hurts
slides.body_md: Same two plans, three levels of EBIT.
bullets: Step 1: work out the **return** on ₹40 lakh.
Step 2: compare it with the **10 per cent** interest.
Step 3: conclude which plan gives higher EPS.

visual.alt: Table of EPS under two plans at three levels of EBIT: at a twenty per cent return the debt plan wins, at ten per cent the plans are equal, at seven and a half per cent the equity plan wins
visual.caption: Trading on equity cuts both ways: it helps only while return exceeds the interest rate.

slides.narration: Now let earnings vary. At a twenty per cent return the debt plan wins. At exactly ten per cent, equal to the interest rate, both plans give the same earnings per share. At seven and a half per cent, the debt plan loses. Trading on equity is a double edged sword.

slides.heading: Quick check: trading on equity
slides.body_md: Trading on equity raises EPS only when…
slides.narration: Compare what borrowed money earns with what it costs.

slides.heading: Fixed capital and its factors
slides.body_md: **Fixed capital** is invested in **long-term assets**: land, buildings, machinery, vehicles.

rows: Heavy assets are needed before earning
Machines go out of date fast

visual.alt: Table of eight factors affecting fixed capital, when each raises the requirement, and an imagined example

slides.narration: Fixed capital buys assets that serve the firm for many years. How much is needed depends on the nature and scale of the business, the technique chosen, how fast technology changes, growth plans, diversification, whether assets can be leased, and whether facilities can be shared with other firms.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: reading choices
slides.body_md: Three choices by an imagined lens company.
bullets: Step 1: name the **factor**.
Step 2: state whether fixed capital **rises or falls**.

visual.alt: Worked table of three choices by an imagined lens company, the factor each shows and whether fixed capital rises or falls
visual.caption: Name the factor first, then state the direction of the effect.

slides.narration: Adding sunglasses and contact lenses is diversification, so more fixed capital is needed. Leasing vans is a financing alternative, so less is needed. Buying a robotic line is a capital intensive technique, so more is needed. Always give the factor and the direction.

slides.heading: Quick check: leasing
slides.body_md: A lab leases a scanner instead of buying it. What happens to its fixed capital requirement?
slides.narration: Does the lab still have to pay for the whole machine at once?

slides.heading: Working capital: permanent and temporary
slides.body_md: **Gross** = total current assets. **Net** = current assets − current liabilities. **Permanent** = year-round minimum. **Temporary** = seasonal extra.

slides.narration: Working capital pays for stock, debtors and cash. Gross working capital is the total of current assets; net deducts current liabilities. In the chart, the flat floor is permanent working capital, needed all year. The hump in the festival months is temporary working capital, needed only for that season.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: net working capital
slides.body_md: An imagined utensil wholesaler's current items.
bullets: Step 1: add the **current assets**.
Step 2: add the **current liabilities**.
Step 3: subtract to get **net working capital**.

visual.alt: Worked table for an imagined utensil wholesaler: current assets of nine lakh forty thousand rupees less current liabilities of five lakh sixty thousand rupees give net working capital of three lakh eighty thousand rupees
visual.caption: Gross = total current assets; net = gross less current liabilities.

slides.narration: Add stock, debtors and cash to get gross working capital of nine lakh forty thousand rupees. Add creditors and wages due to get current liabilities of five lakh sixty thousand. The difference, three lakh eighty thousand rupees, is net working capital.

slides.heading: Factors affecting working capital

rows: The firm is a manufacturer or trader, not a pure service
Stock and cash are used inefficiently
Sales grow, rivals offer more, or prices rise

visual.alt: Table of factors affecting working capital and the condition under which each raises the requirement

slides.narration: Many factors change working capital. Traders and manufacturers need more than service firms. Larger scale, booms and peak seasons need more. A long production cycle, long credit to customers and short credit from suppliers all need more. Inefficiency, scarce raw materials, growth, competition and inflation raise it too.

slides.heading: Quick check: the festival stock
slides.body_md: A garment maker raises stock by ₹4 lakh before festivals and lowers it afterwards. This extra amount is…
slides.narration: Is it needed all year or only for a season?

slides.heading: Fixed capital versus working capital
columns:
**Fixed capital**

Long-term assets; many years; long-term sources; low liquidity.

**Working capital**

Day-to-day operations; within a year; mainly short-term sources; high liquidity.

rows: Mainly short-term: trade credit, bank overdraft

visual.alt: Table distinguishing fixed capital and working capital on purpose, period, sources, liquidity and reversibility of decisions

slides.narration: Fixed capital is locked in long-term assets for many years and should come from long-term sources. Working capital keeps the daily cycle running, turns over within a year, and is mostly financed from short-term sources. Decisions on fixed capital are hard to reverse; working capital is adjusted often.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 2

rows: Helps only when return exceeds interest
Long-term assets; nature, scale, technique and more
Gross, net, permanent, temporary; cycle, credit, season

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 2: capital structure, trading on equity, fixed capital and working capital

slides.narration: To sum up. Capital structure is the mix of debt and equity, decided by cost, return, cash flow, risk, control, flexibility and market conditions. Trading on equity helps only when return beats interest. Fixed capital depends on nature, scale and technique; working capital on cycles, credit and seasons.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: In EPS sums, show **interest, tax, profit after tax and shares** line by line.
Always compare **return on investment** with the **interest rate**.
For fixed or working capital factors, give the **direction**: rises or falls.
Do not mix up **gross** and **net** working capital.

visual.alt: Three steps for case questions: quote the fact, name the factor, and state its effect

slides.narration: Final tips. Lay out EPS working line by line, so method marks are safe. Compare return with interest before praising debt. For each factor, say whether the requirement rises or falls. And remember: gross working capital is total current assets, while net deducts current liabilities.

sections.heading: 2. Financial planning
sections.body_md:
**Financial planning** is the preparation of a **financial blueprint** of an organisation's future operations: an estimate of the funds required, their timing and their sources.

**Objectives:** (i) ensure funds are **available when required**; (ii) see that the firm does **not raise resources unnecessarily**.

**Features of a sound plan:** simplicity; foresight (long-term view); flexibility; optimum use of funds; liquidity; economy (low cost of raising funds); provision for contingencies.

**Importance:** avoids shortage and surplus of funds; links investment and financing decisions; prepares the firm for surprises; reduces waste and duplication; coordinates departments; provides standards for **financial control**.

sections.heading: 3. Capital structure
sections.body_md:
**Capital structure** is the mix of **owners' funds (equity)** and **borrowed funds (debt)** used to finance a business.

**Debt** is usually cheaper (interest is tax-deductible) and does not dilute control, but it carries a **fixed charge** and raises **financial risk**. **Equity** has no fixed charge but is costlier and dilutes control.

**Factors:** cost of debt; cost of equity; tax rate; return on investment (**trading on equity**); cash flow position; business and financial risk; control; flexibility; floatation costs; stock-market conditions; regulatory framework.

**Trading on equity:** using fixed-cost debt to raise EPS. It works only when **return on investment > rate of interest**; otherwise EPS falls.

EPS = (EBIT − interest − tax) ÷ number of equity shares.

sections.heading: 4. Fixed capital
sections.body_md:
**Fixed capital** is the investment in **long-term assets** such as land, buildings, plant, machinery and vehicles. Such decisions involve large sums, last many years and are difficult to reverse.

**Factors affecting fixed capital requirements:**
- **Nature of business** (manufacturing and utilities need more than trading or service firms).
- **Scale of operations.**
- **Choice of technique** (capital-intensive versus labour-intensive).
- **Technology upgradation** (fast-changing machines need frequent replacement).
- **Growth prospects.**
- **Diversification.**
- **Financing alternatives** (leasing reduces the need).
- **Level of collaboration** (sharing facilities reduces the need).

sections.heading: 5. Working capital
sections.body_md:
**Working capital** is the investment in **current assets** — stock, debtors, bills receivable, cash — used for day-to-day operations.
- **Gross working capital** = total current assets.
- **Net working capital** = current assets − current liabilities.
- **Permanent (fixed) working capital:** the minimum level needed throughout the year.
- **Temporary (variable or seasonal) working capital:** the extra needed at peak times.

**Factors:** nature of business; scale; business cycle; seasonal factors; production cycle; credit allowed; credit availed; operating efficiency; availability of raw material; growth prospects; level of competition; inflation.

**Fixed versus working capital:** purpose (long-term assets vs daily operations); period (many years vs within a year); sources (long-term vs mainly short-term); liquidity (low vs high).

Extra current assets needed for a season or peak.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Naming shares or debentures as a source for a sole trader or partnership.
- Saying trading on equity always raises EPS.
- Forgetting tax in EPS calculations.

- Saying long credit **from suppliers** raises working capital (it reduces it).

- 1 mark: correct option, term or figure.
- 2–3 marks: each factor named and linked to the case, with the direction of its effect.
- 5 marks: parts answered separately; calculations laid out line by line; a recommendation backed by facts from the case.

P. It is simple enough for managers to follow.
Q. It is rigid and never changed once made.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** P, R and S. Simplicity, foresight and liquidity are features of a sound plan; rigidity is not, because a good plan is flexible.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A financial plan makes financial control easier.

**Reason (R):** The plan sets targets for raising and using funds, against which actual results can be compared.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true; because the plan provides targets, managers can compare actual figures with it and correct deviations.

questions.stem_md: Financial planning is done once, when the business is set up, and is never revised.
questions.solution_md: **False.** False. The plan is reviewed and revised as costs, sales and business conditions change.

questions.stem_md: Financial planning is the preparation of a financial ___ of the future operations of a business.
questions.solution_md: It is a financial blueprint: an outline of how much money will be needed, when, and from where.

questions.stem_md: Pench Paper Mills, an imagined mill near Nagpur, plans its finance for the next five years, including a new pulping unit, and chooses the cheapest suitable sources. Name and explain the two features of a sound financial plan shown here.
questions.solution_md: Foresight and economy, each linked to the mill.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Foresight (long-term view):** the mill looks **five years ahead** and includes the **new pulping unit** in its plan.
2. **Economy:** it chooses the **cheapest suitable sources**, keeping the cost of raising funds low.

questions.stem_md: Nilgiri Knitwear, an imagined sweater maker in Ooty, sells most of its output from October to January. Explain three ways in which financial planning would help it.
questions.solution_md: Three benefits (timely funds, avoiding surplus, linking investment and financing, control, reducing waste, preparing for shocks) applied to the seasonal firm.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Funds at the right time:** it can arrange money **before** the winter rush to buy wool and pay extra workers.
2. **No idle funds:** after January it can repay short-term loans instead of keeping **surplus cash** that costs interest.
3. **Basis for control:** monthly targets let managers **compare** actual spending and sales with the plan and act early.

questions.stem_md: The financial plan of Vembanad Houseboats (imagined) runs to 90 pages of complex tables, ignores the monsoon off-season and keeps no cash for wages in lean months. Identify three features of a sound plan that are missing and explain each.
questions.solution_md: Simplicity, foresight and liquidity identified from the case, each explained.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Simplicity:** a 90-page plan of **complex tables** is hard for managers to follow; a sound plan is clear.
2. **Foresight:** it **ignores the monsoon** off-season, so it fails to look ahead at a known change.
3. **Liquidity:** it keeps **no cash for wages** in lean months; a sound plan keeps enough liquid funds.

questions.stem_md:
Konkan Cashew Processors (imagined) buys raw nuts in three harvest months, processes them over the year and exports in two shipments.
(a) What is meant by financial planning? [1]
(b) Explain two features of a sound financial plan. [2]
(c) Explain two ways in which financial planning would help this unit. [2]
questions.solution_md: Meaning; two features; two benefits applied to the cashew unit.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Financial planning** is preparing a **financial blueprint** of future operations: estimating **how much** money is needed, **when**, and from **which sources**.

(b) **Flexibility:** the plan can be **adjusted** if nut prices or freight rates change suddenly. **Liquidity:** it keeps enough **cash** to pay workers and bills while the export money is awaited.

(c) **Funds when needed:** the unit can arrange a **seasonal loan before the harvest**, so it buys its full quantity of nuts. **Avoids idle funds:** after the export payments arrive, it can **repay** the loan instead of holding surplus cash that costs interest. The plan also gives monthly targets that managers can use for control.

questions.stem_md: The capital structure of a company refers to

options.text_md: the layout of its factory buildings
the list of its fixed assets
the mix of owners' funds (equity) and borrowed funds (debt) in its long-term finance
the number of its employees in each department

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** the mix of owners' funds (equity) and borrowed funds (debt) in its long-term finance. Capital structure is the proportion of debt and equity used to finance the business.

questions.stem_md: The founders of Pamba Pharma Ltd, an imagined drug maker in Kottayam, hold 52 per cent of its shares and fear losing control. To raise ₹20 crore, they are most likely to prefer

options.text_md: a fresh public issue of equity shares
a rights issue that they cannot subscribe to

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** debentures or a term loan. Debt holders have no voting rights, so borrowing keeps the founders' control intact; new equity would dilute it.

questions.stem_md: Kaziranga Eco Lodges, an imagined resort company in Assam, earns almost all its income between November and April and very little in the flood season. When choosing its capital structure it should be cautious about

options.text_md: large debt with fixed monthly interest

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** large debt with fixed monthly interest. Interest must be paid every period whatever the earnings; uneven cash flows make heavy debt risky.

questions.stem_md: Why is debt usually a cheaper source of long-term funds than equity for a profitable company?

options.text_md: Debt holders share in the profits of the company
Debt never has to be repaid
Interest on debt is a tax-deductible expense, while dividends are paid out of profit after tax
Equity shareholders always receive a fixed dividend

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Interest on debt is a tax-deductible expense, while dividends are paid out of profit after tax. Interest reduces taxable profit, so the effective cost of debt falls; dividends give no such tax saving.

questions.stem_md: Tunga Tractors Ltd, an imagined company in Shivamogga, could borrow more today but chooses to keep part of its borrowing capacity unused so that it can raise loans quickly if a good opportunity arises. Which factor of capital structure is it considering?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Flexibility. Keeping borrowing power in reserve allows the firm to raise funds quickly later: flexibility.

questions.stem_md: Trading on equity raises the earnings per share only when

options.text_md: the return on investment is higher than the rate of interest on debt
the rate of interest is higher than the return on investment

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** the return on investment is higher than the rate of interest on debt. Borrowed money adds to EPS only if it earns more than it costs; otherwise EPS falls.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** For a profitable company, debt is generally a cheaper source of finance than equity.

**Reason (R):** Interest on debt is not allowed as a deduction while computing taxable profit.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The assertion is true. The reason is false: interest is a deductible expense, which is one reason debt is cheaper.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Trading on equity always increases the earnings per share.

**Reason (R):** Interest on debt has to be paid only in years when the company earns a profit.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Both are false. Trading on equity raises EPS only when the return on investment exceeds the interest rate, and interest is a fixed charge payable even in a loss year.

questions.stem_md: A higher proportion of debt in the capital structure increases the financial risk of a company.
questions.solution_md: **True.** True. More debt means larger fixed interest and repayment obligations, which raise the chance of default if earnings fall.

questions.stem_md: Complete the analogy. Equity shares : Owners' funds :: Debentures : ___
questions.solution_md: Equity shares represent owners' funds; debentures represent borrowed funds (debt).

questions.stem_md: Godavari Glassworks Ltd, an imagined company in Rajahmundry, needs ₹40,00,000. Under Plan A it issues 4,00,000 equity shares of ₹10 each and borrows nothing. Its expected earnings before interest and tax are ₹8,00,000 and the tax rate is 25 per cent. Calculate its earnings per share under Plan A (in ₹).
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: No debt, so interest = 0 and EBT = ₹8,00,000.
Step 2: Tax = 25 per cent of 8,00,000 = ₹2,00,000; EAT = ₹6,00,000.
Step 3: EPS = 6,00,000 ÷ 4,00,000 = ₹1.5.

questions.stem_md: Under Plan B, Godavari Glassworks Ltd (imagined) raises the same ₹40,00,000 as ₹20,00,000 of debentures at 10 per cent interest and 2,00,000 equity shares of ₹10 each. With the same EBIT of ₹8,00,000 and tax at 25 per cent, calculate its earnings per share under Plan B (in ₹).
Godavari Glassworks Ltd (imagined) earns 20 per cent on its capital and can borrow at 10 per cent. What is trading on equity, and should it use more debt?
questions.solution_md: Meaning, and the condition ROI > interest rate applied.

answer.model_answer_md: **Trading on equity** means using **fixed-cost debt** along with equity to **raise earnings per share**. Yes: its **return (20 per cent) exceeds the interest rate (10 per cent)**, so each borrowed rupee earns more than it costs.

questions.stem_md: Pamba Pharma Ltd (imagined) has steady cash flows from its long-selling cough syrup, and its founders want to keep control. Explain two factors that favour more debt in its capital structure.
questions.solution_md: Cash flow and control, each linked to the company.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Cash flow position:** **steady cash** from the cough syrup means it can meet **fixed interest** and repayments safely.
2. **Control:** debenture holders get **no voting rights**, so borrowing keeps the founders' **control** intact.

questions.stem_md: Tunga Tractors Ltd (imagined) is choosing between debt and equity. Its sales swing with the monsoon, share prices are currently depressed, and the corporate tax rate has just risen. Explain how each of these three facts affects its capital structure decision.
questions.solution_md: Each fact linked to its factor (cash flow, market conditions, tax) and its effect on the debt–equity choice.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Uneven cash flow:** sales that swing with the monsoon make **fixed interest risky**, which argues for **less debt**.
2. **Stock-market conditions:** with **depressed share prices**, a new equity issue would raise little, so **debt** looks more practical now.
3. **Tax rate:** a **higher tax rate** increases the tax saving on interest, making **debt cheaper**.

questions.stem_md: Suppose the EBIT of Godavari Glassworks Ltd (imagined) falls to ₹3,00,000. Using its two plans (Plan A: 4,00,000 shares, no debt; Plan B: 2,00,000 shares and ₹20,00,000 debt at 10 per cent; tax 25 per cent), calculate EPS under each plan and explain the result.
questions.solution_md: Plan A EPS ₹0.5625; Plan B EPS ₹0.375; ROI below interest rate, so debt reduces EPS.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Plan A:** EAT = 3,00,000 − 75,000 = **₹2,25,000**; EPS = **₹0.5625**.
**Plan B:** EBT = 3,00,000 − 2,00,000 = ₹1,00,000; EAT = **₹75,000**; EPS = **₹0.375**.
Now the **return (7.5 per cent) is below the 10 per cent interest**, so debt **lowers** EPS: trading on equity works against shareholders.

marking_scheme.step: Explanation using ROI and interest rate

questions.stem_md:
Godavari Glassworks Ltd (imagined) needs ₹40,00,000. Plan A: 4,00,000 equity shares of ₹10. Plan B: 2,00,000 equity shares of ₹10 and ₹20,00,000 debentures at 10 per cent. Expected EBIT is ₹8,00,000; tax is 25 per cent. Its glass sales are steady and the promoters own most of the shares.
(a) Calculate EPS under both plans. [2]
(b) Recommend a plan, giving three reasons from the facts. [3]
questions.solution_md: EPS ₹1.5 (A) and ₹2.25 (B); Plan B justified by trading on equity, cash flow and control. At EBIT ₹4,00,000 both plans give EPS ₹0.75.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Plan A:** EBT ₹8,00,000; tax ₹2,00,000; EAT ₹6,00,000; **EPS = ₹1.5**.
**Plan B:** interest ₹2,00,000; EBT ₹6,00,000; tax ₹1,50,000; EAT ₹4,50,000; **EPS = ₹2.25**.

(b) **Plan B is recommended.**
1. **Trading on equity:** the return on capital is **20 per cent**, double the **10 per cent** interest, so debt **raises EPS** from ₹1.5 to ₹2.25.
2. **Steady cash flow:** steady glass sales mean the company can pay the **fixed interest** of ₹2 lakh every year without strain.
3. **Control:** debenture holders have **no voting rights**, so the promoters keep control, while Plan A would bring in twice as many new shareholders.
The firm should still watch its risk if EBIT ever falls below ₹4 lakh, where the two plans give equal EPS.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Recommendation with three reasons from the facts

questions.stem_md: Fixed capital refers to the funds a business invests in

options.text_md: long-term assets such as land, buildings, machinery and vehicles

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** long-term assets such as land, buildings, machinery and vehicles. Fixed capital is invested in assets held for many years, not in assets turned into cash within a year.

questions.stem_md: Which of these imagined businesses will need the **largest** proportion of fixed capital?

options.text_md: A stationery shop near a college
A travel agent who books tickets online
A fruit-juice stall at a bus stand
A company building and running a cable-car line in the hills

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A company building and running a cable-car line in the hills. A cable-car line needs towers, cables, cabins and stations before it earns anything: very heavy fixed assets.

questions.stem_md: Two imagined soap makers produce the same output. One uses a fully automatic plant; the other uses hand moulds and more workers. The automatic plant needs more fixed capital because of

options.text_md: the choice of a capital-intensive technique

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** the choice of a capital-intensive technique. A capital-intensive technique relies on machines, so it needs more fixed capital than a labour-intensive one.

questions.stem_md: Instead of buying a ₹2 crore scanner, Doon Diagnostics (imagined) takes it on a five-year lease and pays monthly rent. The effect on its fixed capital requirement is that it

options.text_md: rises, because rent must be paid
is unchanged, because the scanner is still used
falls, because a financing alternative replaces outright purchase

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** falls, because a financing alternative replaces outright purchase. Leasing is a financing alternative that lets a firm use an asset without buying it, so less fixed capital is needed.

questions.stem_md: Three imagined dairy cooperatives in a district share one chilling plant instead of building one each. Which factor of fixed capital requirement does this show?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Level of collaboration. Sharing facilities with other firms reduces each firm's fixed capital: level of collaboration.

questions.stem_md: Lonar Lenses Ltd (imagined) expects demand for its lenses to double in three years, so it builds a larger plant now. True or false: a firm with higher growth prospects generally needs more fixed capital.
questions.solution_md: **True.** True. Firms expecting growth build extra capacity in advance, which needs more fixed capital.

questions.stem_md: Sabarmati Steel Tubes Ltd, an imagined Ahmedabad company, is a large-scale maker whose rolling mills must be replaced every few years with newer models. Explain two factors that raise its fixed capital needs.
questions.solution_md: Scale and technology upgradation, each linked to the steel firm.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Scale of operations:** a **large-scale** tube maker needs big mills, sheds and cranes, so more fixed capital.
2. **Technology upgradation:** mills that become **obsolete quickly** must be replaced often, adding to fixed capital.

questions.stem_md: Lonar Lenses Ltd (imagined) is adding contact lenses and sunglasses to its range, will lease its new delivery vans, and is buying a robotic polishing line. Explain how each of these three choices affects its fixed capital requirement.
questions.solution_md: Each choice matched to its factor and the direction of its effect.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Diversification:** adding **contact lenses and sunglasses** needs new machines and space, so fixed capital **rises**.
2. **Financing alternatives:** **leasing the vans** avoids buying them, so fixed capital **falls**.
3. **Choice of technique:** a **robotic** line is capital-intensive, so fixed capital **rises**.

questions.stem_md: Gross working capital means

options.text_md: the total investment in current assets
the share capital of the firm

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** the total investment in current assets. Gross working capital is total current assets; net working capital deducts current liabilities.

questions.stem_md: Gomti Garments, an imagined Lucknow kurta maker, always keeps at least ₹6 lakh in cloth, thread and cash, even in its slowest month. This minimum amount is its
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** permanent working capital. The minimum level of current assets needed throughout the year is permanent (fixed) working capital.

questions.stem_md: Before Eid and Diwali, Gomti Garments (imagined) raises its stock of cloth and finished kurtas by ₹4 lakh above its usual minimum, and brings it back down after the festivals. This extra ₹4 lakh is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** temporary (seasonal) working capital. Extra current assets needed only for a season are temporary, also called variable or seasonal working capital.

questions.stem_md: Ujjain Utensils, an imagined steel-utensil wholesaler, allows shopkeepers 60 days to pay but must pay its own suppliers within 15 days. Its working capital requirement will be

options.text_md: higher, because money is locked in debtors longer than credit is received
lower, because sales are on credit
unchanged, because credit does not affect working capital
zero, because it is a wholesaler

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** higher, because money is locked in debtors longer than credit is received. Giving long credit while getting short credit ties up more funds in current assets, raising working capital needs.

questions.stem_md: An imagined boat-building yard takes nine months to finish each trawler; an imagined bakery turns flour into bread overnight. With equal sales, which statement is correct?

options.text_md: The bakery needs more working capital because its goods perish
The boatyard needs more working capital because of its longer production cycle
Both need the same working capital because sales are equal

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The boatyard needs more working capital because of its longer production cycle. A longer production cycle keeps funds tied up in materials and work-in-progress for longer, so more working capital is needed.

questions.stem_md:
Which of these would **increase** a firm's working capital requirement?
P. A long production cycle
Q. Liberal credit allowed to customers
R. Long credit received from suppliers
S. A boom in business activity
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** P, Q and S. A long cycle, liberal credit to buyers and a boom all raise working capital needs; long credit from suppliers reduces them.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** During a boom, a manufacturing firm generally needs more working capital.

**Reason (R):** Working capital is the money invested in current assets such as stock and debtors.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true, but the reason only defines working capital. The explanation is that in a boom sales and production rise, needing more stock and debtors.

questions.stem_md: Net working capital is the excess of current assets over current liabilities.
questions.solution_md: **True.** True. Net working capital = current assets − current liabilities.

questions.stem_md: Complete the analogy. Delivery van : Fixed capital :: Stock of raw cotton : ___
questions.solution_md: A van is a long-term asset financed by fixed capital; a stock of raw cotton is a current asset financed by working capital.

questions.stem_md: Ujjain Utensils (imagined) has stock ₹4,20,000, debtors ₹3,10,000 and cash ₹2,10,000. It owes creditors ₹3,90,000 and wages ₹1,70,000. Calculate its net working capital (in ₹).
Match each term about working capital with its meaning.

match_right.text_md: Extra current assets needed for a season
Minimum current assets needed all year

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(q), (b)–(s), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). Gross is the total; net deducts current liabilities; permanent is the year-round minimum; temporary is the seasonal extra.

questions.stem_md: Gomti Garments (imagined) needs at least ₹6 lakh of current assets all year and ₹10 lakh in the festival months. Distinguish its permanent and temporary working capital, with amounts.
questions.solution_md: Permanent ₹6 lakh (year-round minimum); temporary ₹4 lakh (seasonal extra).

answer.model_answer_md: **Permanent working capital** is the **minimum ₹6 lakh** it needs throughout the year. **Temporary working capital** is the **extra ₹4 lakh** (₹10 lakh − ₹6 lakh) needed only in the **festival months**.

questions.stem_md: Konkan Cashew Processors (imagined) buys a whole year's nuts in three months, takes several weeks to shell and grade them, and gives foreign buyers 60 days to pay. Explain three factors that raise its working capital needs.
questions.solution_md: Raw-material availability, production cycle and credit allowed, each linked to the case.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Availability of raw material:** nuts are available only in **three harvest months**, so a year's stock must be bought and financed at once.
2. **Production cycle:** shelling and grading take **several weeks**, keeping funds tied in work-in-progress.
3. **Credit allowed:** **60 days' credit** to buyers locks money in debtors.

questions.stem_md: Majuli Mask Makers, an imagined craft partnership in Assam, owns a workshop and also keeps bamboo, paint and cash. Distinguish its fixed capital from its working capital on purpose, period and sources.
questions.solution_md: Three differences, each with the firm's example.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Purpose:** fixed capital buys the **workshop and tools**; working capital pays for **bamboo, paint and wages**.
2. **Period:** fixed capital stays invested for **many years**; working capital **turns over** within a year.
3. **Sources:** fixed capital comes from **long-term** sources such as partners' capital; working capital mostly from **short-term** sources such as trade credit.

questions.stem_md:
Ujjain Utensils (imagined) is a wholesaler. It allows shopkeepers 60 days' credit, gets only 15 days from suppliers, stocks extra goods before the wedding season, and expects sales to grow fast.
(a) Distinguish between gross and net working capital. [1]
(b) Explain four factors that affect its working capital requirement. [4]
questions.solution_md: Gross versus net; four factors (credit allowed, credit availed, seasonality, growth) applied.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Gross working capital** is the **total of current assets**; **net working capital** is **current assets minus current liabilities**.

(b) **Credit allowed:** giving shopkeepers **60 days** to pay locks a large sum in debtors, raising working capital.
**Credit availed:** getting only **15 days** from suppliers means it must pay quickly, so it needs more of its own funds.
**Seasonal factors:** stocking extra utensils **before the wedding season** needs temporary working capital for those months.
**Growth prospects:** as **sales grow**, the wholesaler must carry more stock and more debtors, so its working capital must rise along with them.

questions.stem_md:
Kaziranga Eco Lodges Ltd (imagined) owns cottages, boats and jeeps, and also buys food, fuel and linen every week of the tourist season.
(a) Give two differences between its fixed capital and working capital. [2]
(b) Explain three factors that affect the fixed capital requirement of a resort company like this. [3]
questions.solution_md: Two differences; three factors (nature, scale, financing alternatives, technique, growth, diversification, collaboration) applied.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Nature of assets:** fixed capital is tied up in **cottages, boats and jeeps**, used for years; working capital is held in **food, fuel and linen**, used up within the season. **Sources:** fixed capital should come from **long-term** funds such as shares; working capital comes largely from **short-term** funds such as trade credit.

(b) **Nature of business:** a resort must own **land, cottages and vehicles** before guests arrive, so it needs heavy fixed capital. **Scale:** more cottages and safari jeeps mean **more fixed capital**. **Financing alternatives:** it could **lease jeeps** or hire boats instead of buying them, reducing its fixed capital, and keep its own funds for building more cottages.

**(a)** **Correct option: (d)** Admitting a new partner. In a partnership, a new partner who brings capital is a source of owners' funds.

**(b)** 18 − 8 − 6 = ₹4 lakh.

**(c) (i)** Foresight and liquidity from the passage.

**OR (c) (ii)** One advantage and one limitation of owners' funds in a partnership.

**(b)** Partners bring 4 × ₹2 lakh = ₹8 lakh and the curator ₹6 lakh, so the loan must cover **₹4 lakh**.

questions.passage_md:
**Majuli Mask Makers (imagined), Assam**

Four partners make painted bamboo masks for museums and theatre groups. Orders have grown, and they now want a larger workshop costing ₹18 lakh. Partner Bornali suggests each partner bring ₹2 lakh more and that they invite a retired museum curator to join with ₹6 lakh. Partner Hemanta wants a bank loan for the rest. Bornali also prepares a two-year money plan showing when each instalment for the workshop falls due and keeps a cushion for paint and wages in the slow monsoon months.

children.stem_md: Inviting the retired curator to join with ₹6 lakh is an example of which source of finance?
children.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Admitting a new partner. In a partnership, a new partner who brings capital is a source of owners' funds.

children.stem_md: How much of the ₹18 lakh will Hemanta's bank loan have to cover?

answer.model_answer_md: Partners bring 4 × ₹2 lakh = ₹8 lakh and the curator ₹6 lakh, so the loan must cover **₹4 lakh**.

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Identify two features of a sound financial plan in Bornali's two-year plan.
children.solution_md: Foresight and liquidity from the passage.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Foresight:** it looks **two years ahead** and shows when each instalment falls due.
2. **Liquidity:** it keeps a **cushion for paint and wages** in the slow monsoon months.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Explain one advantage and one limitation of financing the workshop mainly through partners' capital.
alternatives.solution_md: One advantage and one limitation of owners' funds in a partnership.

answer.model_answer_md: **Advantage:** partners' capital carries **no interest** and need not be repaid on a fixed date. **Limitation:** the amount is limited by the **partners' own savings**, so a loan is still needed.

questions.stem_md: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow. *(Imagined company and figures, written by SOYL for practice.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** **Correct option: (d)** fixed capital requirement. Panels, land and inverters are long-term assets: fixed capital.

**(b)** Nature of business: little stock, steady receipts.

**(c) (i)** Trading on equity and cash flow from the passage.

**OR (c) (ii)** One financial risk and one sensible safeguard.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (d) fixed capital requirement

**(b)** It needs only a **small stock of spare parts**; there are no raw materials to buy or goods to stock.

**(c) (i)** 1. **Trading on equity:** expected **return of 13 per cent exceeds the 9 per cent** interest, so debt raises EPS.
2. **Cash flow:** **steady monthly receipts** under the 25-year contract make fixed interest safe to pay.

**OR (c) (ii)** **Risk:** if the state **delays payments**, fixed interest and repayments may still fall due, causing **default**. **Way to reduce it:** keep a **reserve** of cash or some unused borrowing capacity (flexibility).

questions.passage_md:
**Thar Solar Parks Ltd (imagined), Jodhpur**

Thar Solar Parks is building a 50-megawatt solar farm. Panels, land and inverters will cost ₹180 crore. Power is sold to the state under a 25-year contract, so the company expects steady monthly receipts. It needs only a small stock of spare parts and some cash for salaries and cleaning crews.
